records.our_prose: The most important companion for a pawpaw is another pawpaw. Pawpaw cannot pollinate itself, so a single tree, or a group of trees that are all the same variety or all suckers from one plant, will flower but set little or no fruit. Plant at least two genetically different pawpaws (two different named varieties, or two or more seedlings) close together so their flowers can cross-pollinate. Beyond that second tree, what matters most is the root zone: keep grass and weeds pulled back from under a young tree, since lawn competes hard for water, and remember pawpaw is a woodland tree that wants shade over its roots and its young leaves for the first year or two.

records.our_prose: Pawpaw (Asimina triloba) is a deciduous understory tree native to eastern North America and, in the Annonaceae (custard-apple) family, the largest edible fruit native to the continent. Its custardy, tropical-tasting fruit, a blend of banana, mango, and pineapple, ripens in late summer and fall and is so perishable it is almost never sold in stores. Growing it well means working with two unusual traits: it is self-incompatible and fly- and beetle-pollinated, so it needs two genetically distinct trees and often hand pollination to set fruit; and as a woodland understory native, its young foliage wants part shade the first year or two before it takes full sun. It is very cold-hardy across roughly zones 5 to 8, spreads by root suckers into clonal patches, and is notably free of the pests and diseases that plague other fruit trees, with deer avoiding its foliage.

records.our_prose: A balanced ratio such as 10-10-10 suits pawpaw; on fertile, organic-rich ground it may need no feeding at all. Kentucky State recommends a balanced feed (a 20-20-20 is often cited) applied lightly and often to young trees during the first half of the season. Avoid heavy nitrogen, which pushes soft growth at the expense of a sturdy framework.

records.our_prose: Pawpaw grows under other trees in the woods, and its young leaves burn easily in strong sun, so a young tree moved straight into full sun can scorch. For the first year or two, give it part shade (shade cloth, a taller plant nearby, or a dappled spot) and keep the soil evenly moist under a thick mulch. This is unusual for a fruit tree, but it is how a young pawpaw makes it; it wants full sun only once it is established.

records.our_prose: Hardening off (slowly getting a plant used to the outdoors) works a little differently for pawpaw. You plant it in spring from a pot, and its young leaves burn easily in strong sun, so for the first year or two give it a shady or part-shade spot and let it get used to brighter light slowly. Do not move a shade-grown young pawpaw straight into a hot, open, sunny place.

records.our_prose: Choose pawpaw varieties differently from other fruit trees: the first rule is genetic diversity, not chill matching. Because the species is self-incompatible, plant at least two different cultivars (or a cultivar plus seedlings) with overlapping bloom so their flowers can cross-pollinate. Named grafted cultivars, most famously the Peterson selections (Shenandoah, Susquehanna, Allegheny, Potomac) and old standards like Sunflower and Overleese, give larger fruit, fewer seeds, and better flavor than random seedlings, and they bear sooner. Chill requirement is estimated at roughly 400 to 1000 hours and is not well differentiated among cultivars, so match your winters loosely and prioritize two compatible, overlapping-bloom trees.

records.our_prose: The two most important times to keep the tree watered are the first two years after planting, when a young pawpaw can die if it dries out, and midsummer while the fruit is filling, when dryness leads to small fruit and fruit drop. Keep the water steady through both. Unlike some fruit trees, pawpaw wants even moisture the whole time it has leaves.

records.our_prose: The first year is about helping the tree settle in, not getting fruit. Plant a potted tree in spring without disturbing its deep taproot, shade the young leaves (which burn in full sun) for the first year or two, keep the soil evenly moist under a thick mulch, and pull off any flowers that form. Plant at least two different trees so they can pollinate each other once they start fruiting. Go easy on fertilizer; a light balanced feeding helps a young tree, but do not push soft growth late in the year.
